newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: High NZ dollar cuts seafood exports by 5 percent.
newsitem.headline: High NZ dollar cuts seafood exports by 5 percent.

text.p: Overvaluation of the NZ dollar cut export earnings from seafood by $60 million or nearly 5 percent in 1996, the NZ Fishing Industry Board said on Friday.
Exports fell to $1.18 billion, down 4.74 percent from $1.24 billion in 1995.
The volume of seafood exports rose 1.4 percent, meaning that the simple average return for each tonne of fish and fisheries products exported fell by 6.1 percent.
"The export results bear out the pain being felt by the fishing industry from the overvalued New Zealand dollar," deputy chief executive Alastair Macfarlane said.
The export figures demonstrated a disturbing trend in seafood sales with growth in added value products becoming very hard to sustain, he said.

"Total earnings from prepared fish products fell nearly 18 percent and the average return for frozen filleted fish fell 12 percent. On the other hand, the volume of fish exported in relatively unprocessed forms -- whole, or headed and gutted -- increased nearly 19 percent, while the total earnings from these product forms increased only 4 percent.

"In other words seafood exporters are finding it hard to sustain added value production and exports. But when they revert to less processed product forms, their returns are dropping there also. They are being hit from both sides," he said.

At the same time as export returns were being hit by the high NZ dollar, the seafood industry was having to cope with government charges to recover fee costs of fisheries management and research which took out around 7 percent of the value of fish at the point when it is caught, Macfarlane said.
